INSERT INTO course_lessons (moduleId, slug, title, orderIndex, content, linkedScenarioId, estimatedMinutes, isPublished) VALUES (30005, 'electrical-measurement-strategy', 'Electrical Measurement Strategy: What to Measure and Why', 2, '## Your Meter Is Your Most Powerful Diagnostic Tool

A multimeter in the hands of a skilled troubleshooter is like a stethoscope in the hands of a doctor. It doesn''t just give you numbers—it tells you a story. But only if you know what to measure, where to measure it, and how to interpret the results.

This lesson covers the measurement strategies that separate expert troubleshooters from parts-swappers.

## The Three Fundamental Measurements

Every electrical fault can be diagnosed with three types of measurements:

| Measurement | What It Tells You | When to Use It |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Voltage (VAC/VDC) | Is power present? Is it the right level? | First measurement—always start here |
| Current (Amps) | Is the load drawing normal current? | When voltage is correct but something isn''t working right |
| Resistance (Ohms) | Is the path complete? Is insulation intact? | When power is OFF—verifying wiring and components |

## Voltage Measurement Strategy

### The "Work Backward from the Load" Method

When a motor, solenoid, or other load isn''t operating, start at the load and work backward toward the source:

1. **Measure across the load terminals.** If you have proper voltage here and the load isn''t operating, the load itself is bad.
2. **If no voltage at the load,** move upstream to the next switching device (contactor, relay, fuse).
3. **Measure input vs. output of each device.** Voltage on the input but not the output = that device is open.

This method guarantees you find the open circuit in minimum measurements.

### Voltage Levels and What They Mean

| Reading | Interpretation | Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 VAC across load | No power reaching load—open circuit upstream | Work backward to find the open |
| 120 VAC across load (should be running) | Load is open (burned coil, broken wire at terminal) | Check load resistance with power off |
| 85 VAC (should be 120) | Voltage drop—high resistance connection or overloaded source | Check connections, measure at source |
| 480 VAC between phases (should be 480) | Normal—problem is elsewhere | Move to current measurement |
| 480 VAC on two phases, 0 on third | Single-phasing—blown fuse or open contactor pole | Check fuses and contactor contacts |

## Current Measurement Strategy

### When Voltage Is Correct But Something Is Wrong

If you have proper voltage at the load but the system isn''t behaving correctly, current tells you what''s happening inside the load:

- **Zero amps with voltage present:** Open circuit inside the load (broken winding, open thermal protector)
- **Higher than nameplate amps:** Mechanical overload, bearing failure, misalignment, or voltage imbalance
- **Lower than expected amps:** Unloaded condition (broken coupling, slipping belt, empty pump)
- **Fluctuating amps:** Intermittent connection, varying load, or mechanical issue (bad bearing, misalignment)

### Current Imbalance on Three-Phase Motors

On a three-phase motor, measure all three phases. They should be within 2-3% of each other.

| Phase A | Phase B | Phase C | Diagnosis |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15A | 15.2A | 14.8A | Normal (< 2% imbalance) |
| 15A | 15A | 22A | Voltage imbalance or shorted turns on Phase C winding |
| 15A | 0A | 15A | Single-phasing—Phase B fuse blown or contactor pole open |
| 25A | 24A | 26A | All high—mechanical overload (check coupling, bearings, load) |

> **CRITICAL SAFETY NOTE:** Never measure current by breaking the circuit and inserting your meter in series on anything above 24VDC/24VAC. Use a clamp-on ammeter. Inserting a meter in series on a 480V motor circuit with the meter set to amps will cause an arc flash explosion.

## Resistance Measurement Strategy

### The Golden Rule: Power Must Be OFF

Measuring resistance on an energized circuit will damage your meter and give meaningless readings. Always verify the circuit is de-energized before switching to ohms.

### What Resistance Tells You

- **Motor windings:** Each phase should read the same (within 5%). Infinite = open winding. Zero = shorted winding. Megohms to ground = good insulation.
- **Fuses:** Should read near zero ohms. Any reading above 1 ohm = blown fuse.
- **Relay/contactor coils:** Should read the rated coil resistance (typically 20-200 ohms for 120VAC coils). Infinite = open coil.
- **Wire runs:** Should read near zero. High resistance = damaged wire, corroded terminal, or loose connection.
- **Sensors:** NTC thermistors decrease resistance with temperature. PTC thermistors increase. RTDs have a known resistance at a known temperature (100 ohms at 0C for Pt100).

## Measurement Sequence for Common Faults

### Motor Won''t Start

1. Check for voltage at motor terminals (all 3 phases)
2. If no voltage: check contactor output, then input, then control circuit
3. If voltage present: check motor resistance (phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground)
4. If motor resistance OK: check for mechanical binding (try to rotate shaft by hand)

### VFD Faulted

1. Read the fault code on the display (this IS your first measurement)
2. Check input power to the VFD (all 3 phases at input terminals)
3. Check DC bus voltage (if accessible—should be ~650VDC for 480V input)
4. If output fault: disconnect motor and measure motor insulation resistance
5. Check for ground faults (phase-to-ground on output wiring)

### PLC Output Not Energizing

1. Check the output status in the program (is the rung TRUE?)
2. If rung is TRUE but output LED is off: output module fault or blown fuse on output card
3. If output LED is on but field device isn''t working: measure voltage at the output terminal
4. If voltage at terminal but device dead: problem is in field wiring or the device itself

## The Measurement Log

Expert troubleshooters write down their measurements. Not because they have bad memories, but because:

- It prevents re-measuring the same point
- It reveals patterns ("every measurement downstream of TB-4 is zero...")
- It provides documentation for the work order
- It helps the next technician if the problem recurs

In the simulator, your measurement history is tracked automatically. In the real world, carry a notepad or use your phone.', 12, 25, 1);
